sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You rewatch your favorite movie for comfort. That familiar repetition is actually a tool for cognitive preservation. In 2020, Dr. Allison Allison and researchers at the University of Exeter monitored about 40 Asian small-clawed otters juggling pebbles. Why do these animals spend hours tossing rocks? The researchers expected play to help young otters practice hunting skills. The result? Juggling did not help them extract food from complex puzzle boxes any faster. Instead, elderly otters juggled far more when they were hungry. That's it. It keeps their aging brains sharp and distracts them from empty stomachs. Was this behavior isolated to just one facility? Other wildlife studies show similar repetitive play across diverse mammal species, a phenomenon known as cognitive enrichment. So why do we assume animal play is just aimless fun? Real evidence shows it actively maintains neurological health during stress. So next time you rewatch your favorite movie for comfort, remember that simple repetition protects your mind. You rewatch your favorite movie for comfort.

claims.claim: Otter pebble juggling is not tied to foraging skill practice, but increases in older otters and when hungry to maintain brain function.

claims.claim: Repetitive animal play acts as cognitive enrichment to protect neurological health during stress.
